sentences.text: Scientists believe that many decisions are made through the accumulation of noisy evidence until a specific threshold or bound is reached.
This theory suggests that an increase in noise should lead to faster decisions and reduced accuracy.
Paradoxically, the model also predicts that higher noise levels will result in higher confidence during the decision-making process.
To test these ideas, researchers developed a novel sensory manipulation designed to mimic the addition of unbiased noise to the motion-selective regions of the visual cortex.
The researchers verified this method using neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT and MST, which are parts of the brain that process visual motion.
The study involved both humans and monkeys to see how they responded to different levels of visual noise.
For both humans and monkeys, increasing the noise induced faster decisions and greater confidence across a range of different stimuli.
Interestingly, these effects occurred even when the accuracy of the subjects was minimally impaired by the added noise.
In the monkeys specifically, high volatility increased confidence despite having a negligible effect on their accuracy.
The magnitude of the effects observed in the experiments was in agreement with the predictions of a bounded evidence accumulation model.
This suggests that the relationship between noise, speed, and confidence can be explained by a common mechanism of bounded evidence accumulation.
The findings show that the brain uses the accumulation of noisy evidence to reach a threshold for various types of perceptual choices.
Because the decision variable diffuses more quickly under high volatility, it leads to the predicted outcome of greater confidence.
By using macaque areas MT and MST to verify the sensory manipulation, the team ensured the noise accurately reflected brain activity changes.
Ultimately, the study demonstrates how humans and monkeys share similar patterns in how noise influences their decision speed and confidence.

sentences.text: The bacterium Shigella flexneri produces an enzyme called OspI that specifically targets a glutamine residue in the host enzyme UBC13 and deamidates it to become glutamate (Q100E).
This deamidation of Q100 to E100 inhibits the synthesis of K63-linked polyubiquitin chains by the UBC13/TRAF6 complex, which prevents the downstream activation of the NF-κB inflammatory response.
When this polyubiquitination activity is silenced, the host's normal immune signaling is effectively shut down.
Researchers found that deamidation weakens the non-covalent interaction of UBC13 with the RING-finger domain of TRAF6 (TRAF6RING) without perturbing the overall UBC13 structure.
The modification inhibited the binding of TRAF6RING to UBC13, but it did not change the fold of UBC13 or its intrinsic E2 activity.
The study revealed that deamidation disrupts both native and transient protein-protein interactions that are usually required for these enzymes to work together.
Specifically, the deamidation-induced intramolecular R14/E100 salt-bridge may interfere with the intermolecular R14/E69 salt-bridge to destabilize the complex.
In this process, the new E100 residue in the modified UBC13 competes with the intermolecular R14/E69 salt-bridge at the interface to form an internal salt-bridge instead.
Furthermore, electrostatic repulsion between E100 and the negatively charged interface of TRAF6RING was observed in the modified UBC13 transient complexes.
While the original UBC13 interface was positively charged, the TRAF6RING interface was negatively charged, and the new glutamate residue creates a repulsive force.
This study provides molecular details of how a post-translational modification can modulate transient protein-protein association to inhibit interaction.
The findings highlight how a pathogen employs subtle mechanisms like salt-bridge competition and the modification of transient complexes to disrupt host cell functions.

sentences.text: Working memory is a vital brain function that relies on the coordination of activity across distant regions of the brain.
Oscillatory activity in the theta frequency range, specifically between 4-7 Hz, appears to organize local groups of neurons across these distant regions during memory processes.
To study this, researchers applied a technique called transcranial alternating current stimulation, or tACS, to the right frontoparietal network.
The researchers used 6 Hz tACS to target specific nodes in the brain, including the middle frontal gyrus and the inferior parietal lobule.
The stimulation was delivered via electrodes placed at specific locations on the scalp known as F4 and P4.
The study found that synchronous tACS improved reaction times for participants during the demanding 2-back task.
This improvement in reaction times made performance on the difficult 2-back task similar to the easier 1-back condition.
The benefits of synchronous stimulation were specifically noted when compared to both desynchronous tACS and a placebo sham stimulation.
Using fMRI scans, the researchers observed that the effects of tACS were highly dependent on the underlying cognitive processing state of the individual.
The results showed that the impact of the electrical current changed based on the relative phase of the stimulation and the internal state of the brain.
During the memory task, synchronous stimulation led to increased activity within the right inferior parietal lobe.
This increased activity in the right inferior parietal lobe correlated with faster responses during the 2-back task.
Furthermore, the synchronous stimulation resulted in increased functional connectivity between the parietal and frontal areas of the brain.
By altering phase synchrony, the researchers were able to shape the information flow and control long-range network interactions.
These findings demonstrate that external synchronization can modulate network dynamics to enhance performance on difficult cognitive tasks.

sentences.text: The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is a brain region that is critical for both spatial and non-spatial behaviors.
Researchers used optogenetic circuit mapping in mice to reveal how parallel circuits in the superficial RSG process different types of inputs.
The anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum are sources of spatial information that strongly and selectively recruit small low-rheobase (LR) pyramidal cells in the RSG.
These LR neurons are the predominant cell type in the RSG for receiving and processing head direction inputs.
In contrast, neighboring regular-spiking (RS) cells are preferentially controlled by inputs from the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex.
The claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex provide the RSG with sources of mostly non-spatial information.
This parallel processing is permitted by precise sublaminar axonal and dendritic arborization within RSG layer 1.
The separation of these circuits depends on the precise colocalization of the dendrites of local principal cells and incoming axons from the thalamus.
Specific synaptic dynamics enable LR neurons to compute the speed of head rotation.
These neurons can compute speed even though the head direction inputs they receive do not explicitly encode speed.
Computational models show that the firing rate of an LR cell receiving these inputs is strongly correlated with angular head speed.
Because of these properties, LR neurons are ideally positioned to contribute to initial spatial orientation computations.
These LR cells serve as the predominant subtype within the RSG for encoding spatial information to support navigation.

sentences.text: The plant species Arabidopsis thaliana consistently produces four petals, a phenotype that is robust to natural genetic variation.
In contrast, the closely related species Cardamine hirsuta shows similar frequencies of each petal number between zero and four in flowers from 39 accessions.
Researchers found that divergence in the pleiotropic floral regulator APETALA1 (AP1) can account for the species-specific difference in petal number robustness.
The Arabidopsis thaliana AP1 gene canalized Cardamine hirsuta petal number by masking the phenotypic effects of at least nine quantitative trait loci (QTL).
These functional differences in AP1 are more likely to reside in regulatory regions of the gene rather than coding sequences.
Despite this, there is sufficient standing genetic variation in natural accessions of Cardamine hirsuta to produce plants with four-petalled flowers.
The study highlights how the Arabidopsis thaliana version of the AP1 gene provides robustness by hiding the effects of other genetic factors.
By masking these nine quantitative trait loci, the gene ensures that the flower consistently develops four petals regardless of other genetic variations.
The variation in Cardamine hirsuta persists even though the species has the genetic potential to produce stable four-petalled flowers through recombination.
Ultimately, the divergence in the regulatory regions of AP1 explains why one species has a fixed petal number while the other remains variable.
This discovery shows how a single regulator like APETALA1 can influence the stability of physical traits across different plant species.

sentences.text: Sulforaphane (SFN) is a natural product produced in cruciferous vegetables after mechanical damage that mobilizes the transcription regulator nuclear erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) to reprogram cellular gene expression.
Researchers found that SFN blocks HIV infection in primary macrophages but does not block infection in primary T cells.
To understand the role of Nrf2, scientists used siRNA-mediated depletion of Nrf2, which boosted HIV infectivity in primary macrophages and reduced the anti-viral effects of SFN treatment.
The study determined that SFN treatment blocks infection after entry into the cell, but before the formation of 2-LTR circles.
Interestingly, the anti-viral proteins SAMHD1 and MX2 were not upregulated during this process, indicating SFN did not significantly change their levels.
The discovery that Nrf2 mobilization counters HIV infection in macrophages stands in contrast with other viruses like Marburg, Dengue, and KSHV, which benefit from increased Nrf2 expression.
This research shows for the first time that Nrf2 action can potently block HIV infection and highlights a novel way to trigger this inhibition in specific immune cells.

sentences.text: Aedes-borne arboviruses, such as dengue and Zika, are causing increasing epidemics and mortality worldwide.
The Dominican Republic experienced a large dengue epidemic in 2015 followed closely by a Zika virus outbreak in 2016.
Data showed that 75% of all dengue cases occurred in people under 20 years old, while Zika cases were more widely distributed across different ages.
Zika infections were highly clustered among females, who accounted for 73.8% of the reported cases.
In contrast, Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) attack rates were slightly higher in males than in females, at 0.62 per 10,000 population.
Evidence suggests that existing dengue immunity had little impact on the reported Zika attack rates at the population level.
The higher reporting of Zika among women of reproductive age is likely due to health-seeking behavior influenced by community awareness campaigns.
Therefore, media campaigns and screening are recommended for women of reproductive age during future Zika outbreaks.

sentences.text: Under nitrogen deprivation, filaments of the cyanobacterium Anabaena undergo a process of development, resulting in a one-dimensional pattern of nitrogen-fixing heterocysts separated by about ten photosynthetic vegetative cells.
To study this, researchers used a chromosomally-encoded translational hetR-gfp fusion to track the transcription factor HetR, which is essential for heterocyst differentiation.
The study found that expression fluctuations of hetR in nearby cells are coupled, with a characteristic spatial range of circa two to three cells.
These correlations between cells predominantly arise from intercellular molecular transfer and less from cell division.

Under nitrogen-rich conditions, the basal expression of the HetR inhibitor PatS, cell-cell communication influenced by the septal protein SepJ, and positive HetR auto-regulation are essential determinants of these fluctuations.
The research also highlights differences in specificity between the septal proteins SepJ and FraC/FraD, as well as differences between the inhibitors PatS and HetN.

Ultimately, multicellular organisms can use cell-cell communication in order to control noise in gene expression, as these fluctuations are key determinants in the decision of cells whether to differentiate or not.

sentences.text: Humans have the ability to learn and store multiple visuomotor mappings, a process known as dual-adaptation, when they receive feedback for each mapping alternately.
In this study, participants performed a target-pointing task on a graphics tablet where researchers manipulated the visual feedback to simulate environmental changes.

The target shapes were morphed along a continuous scale between spiky and circular shapes, requiring participants to point more to the right to hit spiky targets and more to the left to hit round ones.
The researchers developed an implicit Bayesian learning model, which could be described by a Mixture-of-Kalman-Filters, to predict how people generalize these movements through categorization.
The experimental results showed that participants apply the mapping corresponding to the trained shape that has the most similarity to the current one.
This learning process was not automatic, as only those participants who had explicit awareness and consciously noticed the role of the shape were able to learn.
Furthermore, the learning rate for these associations decreased as the number of training pairs increased, making the task much harder when five pairs were used instead of two.
The close match between the Bayesian learning model and the empirical results suggests this model is a possible mechanism for how humans simultaneously learn multiple visuomotor mappings.

sentences.text: Many countries where neglected tropical diseases are common cannot start or expand health programs because they lack the baseline data needed for planning and advocacy.
To address this, researchers developed the Integrated Threshold Mapping (ITM) methodology to simultaneously map lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, schistosomiasis, and soil-transmitted helminths.
The specific purpose of this protocol is to determine if a disease has reached the threshold for public health intervention rather than providing exact prevalence figures.
The team tested the protocol by comparing it to standard WHO mapping methodologies in one district each in Mali and Senegal.
The ITM methodology reached the same conclusions as the standard methods for most diseases but resulted in more targeted intervention recommendations for schistosomiasis.
The study found that the integrated approach was feasible and led to a 31% cost savings in Mali and a 19% cost savings in Senegal.
This new tool is more efficient in its use of transport, time in the field, and human resources compared to non-integrated methods.
